You have to weigh the benefits a person brings against the harm they cause. So, yes, I think it was a mistake. I've said it publicly, and many people have said it too. Sorkin: You said it yourself, you would hire him. The board… Musk: Of course, but who wouldn't? He's one of the most talented entrepreneurial CEOs in history. Who wouldn't want to hire Jensen Huang? Of course, Jensen Huang is clearly not looking for a job. I think he's still a bit shocked by these things. It felt like a movie, like a George R.R. Martin script, where a main character you've become emotionally invested in suddenly disappears—it's quite shocking. Sorkin: What do you think will happen to him in the long run? Have you spoken to him about this privately? Musk: Yes. Sorkin: What did he say to you? What do you think will happen next? Musk: I don't know what will happen next. The decision is, of course, in the hands of the Nvidia board. Above that, perhaps the shareholders; but for shareholders to have any influence, it would likely require either the current board to change its mind or for shareholders to elect the board off at the shareholders' meeting—a rather rare occurrence. So, the board is still the one truly in charge. Sorkin: You're with the president now. Have you spoken to him about this? Musk: We probably shouldn't turn this interview into a "Huang Renxun interview." Sorkin: I know. Musk: Okay. I think the president has publicly stated that he believes Huang Renxun should continue as CEO. Almost everyone I know thinks so too. But ultimately, it was a decision made by Nvidia's board of directors. We're not on the board. I feel pretty stupid for losing the midterm elections. Sorkin: Right. Let me ask you something. I'll be talking about your companies later, SpaceX, Tesla, etc. You strongly supported the Republicans in the midterm elections, and they lost. I'd like to hear your reaction to this defeat: what impact do you think it will have on the country, and what impact will it have on your businesses? Now Texas has a Democratic governor, the first time in a long time. What do you think? Musk: First of all, I think the new governor will actually be quite moderate. I don't think she'll be a far-left governor. Based on everything I've heard so far, I think Texas will be fine under Gina Hinojosa. I think it will be fine in that respect. I do think it's a good thing to have some checks and balances. I didn't elaborate on my goals on X. So what was my real goal? By the way, that goal obviously failed: to get the Republicans 51 seats in the Senate. But obviously, the Republicans were crushed in this election. The money I spent—I think I was pretty stupid, spending so much money and not seeing much effect; of course, maybe it would have been worse without that money. But it really shows that elections in America aren't just about money. You can obviously throw a lot of money into an election and have relatively limited results, and I think that was the case this time. So if I could turn back the clock, I would probably have spent less money. I personally wouldn't have put a lot of energy into this, because my focus is on building SpaceX, Tesla, and those things.

I don't think I need a pardon

Sorkin: I'm asking this to see if you think this will impact your company. Because you hear people like the chairman of the oversight committee saying "go to a lawyer"; you hear the president saying, "If I had to give him a pardon"—referring to you—"I would give him a pardon." I'm asking from a personal perspective.

Musk: By the way, I don't think I need a pardon because I haven't committed any crimes. I understand your question. But some of these people are going a bit too far. Some Democrats, I remember even the incoming Texas House Majority Leader saying I should go to jail. Then someone asked him: What crime? He couldn't name a single crime.

Musk: By the way, I don't think I need a pardon because I haven't committed any crimes.

Musk: By the way, I don't think I need a pardon because I haven't committed any crimes.

Starlink, Starship, and the Future of Multiplanetary

Sorkin: Talk about Starlink. I recently saw that you also plan to do terrestrial phone service. What does this ultimately mean for Verizon, T-Mobile, and AT&T? There are many questions: How easy is it to do? How much will it cost? What do you envision the future look like?

Musk: We want to do something useful in communications. These useful communications services will allow us to fund the development of advanced rockets like Starship. We built Starlink, and its benefit is providing high-bandwidth, low-cost connectivity to areas of the world that didn't exist before. We've already provided high-bandwidth, affordable connectivity to many rural schools and hospitals, and to relief organizations. Countless lives have been saved by Starlink—because ships were sinking at sea, or natural disasters had occurred, and Starlink was the only means of communication. I'm not sure of the exact number, but I think it's probably hundreds. Hundreds of lives were saved because, in natural disasters, or as I just mentioned, for those lost or on airplanes, Starlink was the only means of connectivity. It's all over the internet; you can find out how good Starlink has been by searching online. It's also the first global high-bandwidth system ever built. But Starlink has another important long-term role: we need some way to fund rockets capable of extending life as we know it, extending consciousness beyond Earth, to ensure the long-term survival of humanity, consciousness, and life as we understand it by building self-sustaining cities on the Moon and Mars. Because anything could happen on Earth—nuclear war, a massive meteorite, a supervolcano, or some kind of bioengineered virus. Sorkin: Do you think that kind of thing could really happen? Is that what really drives you? Is it what you fear? Musk: You just need to look at the fossil record, look at how many extinction events have happened—lots of them—and you'll know it's just a matter of time, a "when" rather than a "whether." I categorize these as "defensive reasons": extending life and consciousness beyond Earth. These are all important, like insuring life as a whole, a kind of life insurance that covers everything. But if you ask me what motivates me more than that, I would say: I want to see an exciting future—where we venture out to explore new frontiers, to new star systems, and where science fiction isn't just fiction forever. We should be brave enough to go, like in Star Trek, to places no one has ever been before. Maybe we'll discover some long-extinct alien civilizations, maybe we'll find real aliens we can talk to. Being surrounded by stars, I think, is a future worth looking forward to, an incredibly exciting future. How do you judge whether something in the future is really cool? Ask your children, they'll tell you. There are many problems and difficulties in this world that need to be solved, but life can't just be one miserable problem after another. There must be something that excites you about the future, something that makes you happy when you wake up in the morning, something that makes you eager to see what happens next. Becoming a civilization capable of navigating among the stars is one of those things. Sorkin: Let's go back to telecommunications. One reason for doing all this is to raise funds for that future? But I'd like to ask, the cost itself is enormous. I'm also wondering if you'll eventually buy a telecom company in the US. Those companies' stock prices have fallen, and their profit margins and valuation multiples are far lower than yours. So I'd like to understand the longer-term logic. Musk: I think we already have a plan to achieve widespread, ubiquitous access on Earth, including through mobile phones. We'll start launching SpaceX's second-generation direct-to-cell constellation next year, and I think its bandwidth will be about 40 times that of the current first generation, which is a very large multiple; there will be a third generation after that, and so on. It can connect directly from space to your regular phone without requiring anything to the phone. But there's still one piece of the puzzle missing: if you're indoors, especially with a metal roof, it blocks signals from space. So we need some kind of ground infrastructure to address the situation where people are in buildings with thick roofs. That's where the 800 MHz band we bought comes in. We can build what I call micro-ground stations, very small ground stations, and in one way, bundle them with Starlink terminals to create a network. Basically, instead of erecting those huge cell towers everywhere, we're spreading out a large number of micro base stations in densely populated areas. We already have the design, and I think it will be in production next year—a rather revolutionary microcellular device that can be placed directly on the roof like a Starlink antenna to solve the problem of reaching users inside buildings. By the way, I don't think this means AT&T, Verizon, or any other company will go bankrupt. They might lose some revenue, but I think the future demand for bandwidth will be enormous, and that demand will be primarily driven by superintelligence and robots. They will need far more bandwidth than humans: the peak bandwidth for human speech is only about 100 bits per second, while computers can reach a trillion bits per second. So you'll really need several orders of magnitude more bandwidth to serve future superintelligence and massive numbers of robots. Sorkin: You probably can't talk too much, but obviously the biggest news right now is the potential merger of SpaceX and Tesla. I'm curious: what if the deal falls through? I think everyone believes that eventually a way will be found; but if it doesn't work out, how difficult do you think it will be to operate these businesses separately in the future? Musk: I think both paths are viable. It's just that there's more and more overlap or intersection between SpaceX and Tesla that didn't exist before. If you had asked me five years ago if there was any point in SpaceX and Tesla coming together, I would have said no. People asked me that too, and I said I couldn't see any logic in it. The term "synergy" has been overused and misused. Moreover, mergers where the merged company is actually more valuable than the original two companies combined are relatively rare. What we're seeing now is that artificial intelligence and robotics, or rather, superintelligence (SI) and robotics, are creating this convergence. Both SpaceX and Tesla have large AI software teams. Tesla's AI software team primarily works on real-world AI, used in Tesla's Autopilot and Optimus robots; SpaceX, on the other hand, has AI for large-scale models. Beyond AI software, both Tesla and SpaceX have advanced chip design teams. Looking further ahead, orbital computing power will truly be the direction for large-scale deployment. In the future, the supercomputing power in space will round up to 100%. I know this sounds absurd, but please remember this: I believe that the supercomputing power (remaining on the ground) will eventually account for less than 0.4% of all computing power, therefore orbital computing power will round up to 100%. I think this is a fairly easy prediction to make; it's just a matter of time. Sorkin: So you think it's necessary to combine the two companies to make this happen? Musk: It's not necessary to combine them. But wouldn't they be better together? Probably. This isn't a "merge no matter what" situation. These all require shareholder votes, and success or failure is uncertain—at least for Tesla. Even in my vote at SpaceX, I have to represent other shareholders and can't drag them into a merger that's financially detrimental to them, because I would obviously be sued. So the question is: would SpaceX and Tesla be better together, creating more value than they would have been separately? Does this assumption hold up under scrutiny? That's for the shareholders to decide. But there are so many areas of convergence that didn't exist in the past but are becoming increasingly important for the future.

Mergers shouldn't bring additional rewards

Sorkin: I have a rather pointed question. We asked everyone if they had any questions for you, and one question kept coming up.

It relates to the merger of SpaceX and Tesla, and also to your performance-based compensation package at Tesla: at least under the past arrangement, you could have received that portion of your compensation if the deal had gone through. They repeatedly asked: this was designed so you could control Tesla; now you have complete control of SpaceX. If the deal goes through, do you think you should receive that portion of your compensation? Musk: I don't think I should receive any form of reward simply for doing a merger. That's neither reasonable nor justifiable. The right way to look at any agreement is to ask: what were the parties' original intentions when they reached the agreement? You should honor the agreement and keep your word. So, for example, those Tesla stock options that depend on Tesla's performance: I shouldn't receive those option awards just because of the merger with SpaceX, because that doesn't conform to the original agreement—the agreement was that I could only receive these options because of Tesla's performance, not just because of a merger.

Cybercab and Autonomous Driving

Sorkin: Okay. There's been a lot of talk about cars lately, especially about the Cybertruck. Apparently, you're phasing it out to free up more capacity for ride-sharing services, which I guess will eventually be Cybercab. Do you think you'll continue making cars in the end? By the way, I just ordered a Tesla, but I haven't actually received it yet; the waiting list is really long.

Musk: Which model did you order?

Sorkin: YL (Model Y extended version).

Musk: That's definitely our most popular car. So I think we'll probably convert all Model Y production to Model YL, because that seems to be what most people want. Sorkin: But the question is, do you think you'll still be selling cars to individuals in the future, or once that business takes off, will you only make Cybercab? Musk: No. For us, it's still necessary to make cars that can seat different numbers of people. The Cybercab is two-seater and covers about 90% of passenger mileage. If you look at all passenger mileage, the average number of people in a car is about 1.2, so the two-seater Cybercab covers about 90% of passenger mileage. But we still need autonomous vehicles to handle groups of one family or four or six people. So we plan to make an autonomous version of the Model Y without a steering wheel and pedals to transport groups of six or seven people.

Computing Power Collaboration with Anthropic

Sorkin: I know you have some meetings to attend, and it's morning there. I'll just ask a few quick questions related to AI. You recently said that you think many of these "neoclouds" will become "guppies," and some of them won't be financially viable. I'd like you to elaborate, especially since Anthropic is going public tonight. By the way, I'd also like to hear your thoughts on Anthropic. Interestingly, you once thought this company was terrible to Western civilization, but now they're renting a lot of computing power from you. Musk: Yes. By the way, before we leased any computing power to them, I met with a lot of people at Anthropic, and we didn't just push the deal forward immediately. The fact is, I've known quite a few people at Anthropic since my days at OpenAI. Of the people I've met, none of them triggered my "evil detector." And these are relatively short-term contracts that either party can terminate. If I felt Anthropic was doing something very bad for the world, I would obviously terminate those contracts. Similarly, Anthropic can also terminate contracts, depending on the specific contract, with three to six months' notice. Sorkin: Do you think they will terminate them? Because there's some speculation, supposedly they've told some investors they might. Musk: I don't think they're likely to do that. I spoke with Anthropic, and they told me they're very likely to continue leasing computing power from SpaceX, and in fact, they want significantly more. But they also have to clarify that in the worst-case scenario, if extreme limitations are imposed on what artificial intelligence or superintelligence (SI) can do, they might not be able to use that computing power. However, they told me that in their most probable scenario, they hope to add another 10 gigawatts of computing power from SpaceX. That's a huge number. So far, my interactions with the Anthropic team have been: they seem like good people and principled. They may have some quirks, like we all do, but they seem hardworking and concerned about the future. Frankly, I like these people. So overall, it looks good, and they've certainly made some excellent AI. Opus is a great product.

Are you calm right now?

Sorkin: Perhaps I'll ask you two more philosophical questions. When we last met—I was just curious about your current personal state. Last time we were here, I talked to you about how you said your mind was like a storm. I asked you then if that was an unhappy storm. I'm curious to know what it's like now.

Musk: I think it's not always a storm. Maybe sometimes it's stormy weather, sometimes it's not. I'm not particularly stormy right now. I feel relatively calm.

Sorkin: You feel relatively calm?

Musk: Yes. Sorkin: Elon Musk. Thank you. Thank you very much for the conversation. Musk: Thank you.

data.title: NVIDIA Faces Ransomware Threat, but Breach Claims Remain Unverified
data.description:
A 10-Day Countdown Raises Questions

NVIDIA has been listed on the dark-web extortion website of ransomware group The Gentlemen, which is threatening to release allegedly stolen data within approximately 10 days. The listing, posted on 18 November, includes a countdown timer and a contact channel for ransom negotiations.

However, the group has yet to publish any evidence of the alleged breach. No sample files, data inventory, or technical details identifying the affected systems or business units have been provided. The listing alone does not establish that NVIDIA's internal network has been compromised.

NVIDIA Investigates a Possible Third-Party Incident

NVIDIA said it is investigating an incident that may have affected a third-party partner. The company stated that it has found no indication its own systems or networks were affected and that it continues to monitor the situation.

The statement leaves open the possibility that the incident could involve a supplier, contractor, or external partner rather than NVIDIA's core infrastructure. The relationship between the third-party investigation and The Gentlemen's extortion claim has not yet been conclusively established.

Why Researchers Are Urging Caution

Cybersecurity researchers have cautioned against accepting ransomware claims at face value. The Gentlemen has previously been accused of exaggerating attack claims, misattributing stolen information to organisations, or reusing previously exposed data.

Without verifiable samples, investigators cannot determine the authenticity, origin, sensitivity, or volume of the alleged stolen information. Even if data eventually emerges, further investigation would be required to confirm whether it originated from NVIDIA, a partner, or another source.

The group reportedly operates a ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) model, allowing affiliates to carry out attacks using its tools and infrastructure. Such leak-site listings are commonly used to pressure organisations into negotiations, regardless of whether the full extent of an intrusion has been established.

The Wider Risk of Third-Party Exposure

The incident highlights a persistent cybersecurity challenge: organisations can face data exposure through their wider supply chain, even when their own systems remain uncompromised.

Partners, cloud providers, contractors and software vendors may have access to business information, credentials or operational systems. A security weakness within one of these external environments can potentially create risks for multiple organisations.

Companies should therefore review third-party access privileges, monitor data-sharing arrangements, enforce strong authentication, and ensure that vendors meet cybersecurity and incident-reporting requirements.

Conclusion: A Threat Is Not Proof of a Breach

The NVIDIA case remains an evolving cybersecurity incident, with the ransomware group's allegations yet to be substantiated. The countdown may be intended to increase pressure on the company, but it is not evidence that sensitive information has been stolen.

Until verified data or further official findings emerge, organisations and the public should distinguish between ransomware claims and confirmed security incidents. The case also serves as a reminder that cybersecurity resilience extends beyond an organisation's internal network to every partner and service provider connected to its operations.

data.title: South Korea to Ban Private Lenders From Offering General Personal Loans to Soldiers After Borrowing Jumps 69 Times in Three Years
data.description:
From Barracks Bunks to Borrowed Millions: Why Korea Is Curbing Loans to Soldiers

A corporal posted a request on an online platform that links borrowers with private moneylenders last November.

He was due to leave the army the following June and already owed about 20 million won ($15,000) to banks, savings banks and other lenders.

His question was short:

"Is there anywhere I could get my hands on 5 million won?"

His plea is now a regular sight on such sites, and South Korea's financial regulator has decided to act.

The Financial Supervisory Service (FSS) intends to bar private lenders from offering general-purpose personal loans to active-duty servicemen.

🇰🇷 JUST IN: South Korea plans to restrict high-interest loans to active-duty soldiers after borrowings hit ₩24.2B (~$17M), linked to crypto and online gambling.

— CryptoMeter.io (@CryptoMeterIO) November 15, 2026

How Did Lending to Soldiers Grow So Fast?

The numbers show how quickly the market expanded.

According to the Financial Services Commission, the 30 largest registered loan companies lent 24.2 billion won ($17.5 million) to active-duty servicemen in 2025.

That compares with 350 million won ($254,000) in 2022, a rise of almost 69 times in three years.

Regulators link the jump to easier access to online betting and speculative investment.

Soldiers have been allowed to use smartphones after duty hours since 2020, which has put gambling sites within reach of the barracks.

Higher pay has added to the mix.

A sergeant's monthly compensation has more than doubled, from 676,100 won ($490) in 2022 to 1.5 million won ($1,090) this year.

Why Can Private Lenders Reach Soldiers That Banks Cannot?

Mainstream lenders such as banks and savings banks generally refuse unsecured personal loans to serving soldiers, who cannot provide the usual income documents.

Private lenders have filled the gap by accepting copies of military pay account statements as proof of income.

That practice is the target of the new rule.

The proposal was discussed on 12 November at the fifth meeting of the Financial Consumer Protection Advisory Committee, chaired by FSS Governor Lee Chan-jin, and the regulator confirmed it on 15 November.

The FSS has agreed with the Korea Consumer Loan Finance Association to add the ban to the industry's standard operating guidelines by the end of the year.

Enforcement will rely on industry self-regulation, and the FSS will work with the Financial Services Commission and the banking sector to finalise the details.

Not every loan will be blocked.

Collateralised loans and small emergency cash loans will remain available, as the authorities accept that soldiers may need money quickly for living costs.

How Big Is the Gambling Problem in the Army?

The full extent is hard to measure, but Army figures give some indication.

Military police booked 1,721 servicemen on suspicion of online gambling between 2021 and 2025.

That is a small share of an army of more than 320,000 personnel, yet soldiers say betting is far more common among their peers than the official count suggests.

What Do Debt Relief Applications Show?

Requests for help point to growing strain.

The number of active-duty personnel seeking support from the Credit Counseling & Recovery Service stayed in the 400s each year from 2019 to 2021.

It then rose to 753 in 2022 and 1,015 the following year.

A further 322 had applied by April this year, which puts the annual total on course to approach 1,000.

The size of the debts has grown as well.

Average borrowing among servicemen seeking restructuring was 34.01 million won ($24,700) in 2019 and passed 50 million won ($36,300) in 2022.

It reached 58.63 million won ($42,600) as of April this year.

Is This Only a Military Problem?

Experts caution against treating it as one.

Yang Jun-seok, a professor of economics at the Catholic University of Korea, said,

"Debt among servicemen should be understood as part of the broader problem of mounting debt among young people, rather than as an issue unique to the military. Young people are increasingly exposed to financial risks as they take a more active interest in high-risk assets such as cryptocurrencies."

What Else Is the FSS Planning?

Alongside the lending limits, the FSS plans to widen financial education across the armed forces.

That includes more one-on-one counselling and programmes that warn of the dangers of online gambling and leveraged investing.

Starting today, victims of illegal lending in Korea can apply for help online instead of going to a center in person.
